meta.title: NIS 2 MCP server: what it is and what it does
meta.description: An MCP server connects your own AI assistant to the NIS 2 walkthrough. It reads and fills in as you. Finishing and approving stay in the app.

mcpServer.title: What is an NIS 2 MCP server?
mcpServer.subtitle: An MCP server is the connection through which an AI assistant can work with another program. The nisd2.eu server lets your own assistant, such as Claude or Copilot, read and fill in the NIS 2 walkthrough as the person who connected it. Finishing, deciding and approving stay with people, in the app.

sections.heading: What MCP is, in plain words
paragraphs: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is an open standard that lets an AI assistant use another program: it reads data there and calls functions. The program offers an MCP server for this, and the assistant connects to it.

In December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation's new Agentic AI Foundation, which Anthropic, Block and OpenAI co-founded. Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot Studio can all add MCP servers today. If the assistant your company already uses can too, connect that one.

sections.heading: What the nisd2.eu server does
paragraphs: Every nisd2.eu instance serves its MCP server at /api/mcp, a self-hosted one too, so on nisd2.eu it is https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp. It gives your assistant three tools. With get_walkthrough it reads your walkthrough, with fill_walkthrough_item it fills in, for example suppliers, software, ratings or the text of a policy, and with upload_file it uploads a file as evidence, if it can send files itself, as Claude Code can.

Everything goes through the same checks as in the app. The assistant works as the person who connected it, with exactly their rights. If that person holds the Reviewer or Legal reviewer access role in the team, their assistant reads and fills in nothing.

sections.heading: What it does not do
paragraphs: The assistant finishes no item, decides none and signs nothing. The server has no tool for these steps, nor for deleting a supplier, an asset or a training, or for inviting colleagues. Items already finished, recorded as deliberately not done, or signed it leaves alone.
Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the measures. In the walkthrough it approves at item 7.3, signed in with its own account. A managing director's assistant cannot do that either.

sections.heading: Knowledge about NIS 2, or work in your records
paragraphs: Most MCP servers with NIS 2 in their name that we found in October 2026 are knowledge collections. They answer questions about the law, map requirements to each other or check a domain from the outside. They do not know your company, and they write nothing into your records.
The nisd2.eu server works inside your walkthrough. It reads what your company has already recorded and writes into the lists your management approves at the end.

sections.heading: Who it is for, and how to start
paragraphs: It is meant for companies that use the NIS 2 walkthrough and already use an AI assistant at work. It helps most where the facts already exist in another form, such as an accounts payable list or an inventory.

First an admin turns on “Allow AI assistants for this company” in Settings. You open Settings from the profile menu at the bottom of the left sidebar. Then anyone whose account has the walkthrough unlocked connects their own assistant: enter the address in the assistant, sign in through the browser, allow access. Where no browser is possible, they use “Create key” in Settings to get a key that is valid for 90 days.

We tested both ways with Claude Code. For the browser sign-in, run the command below, then type /mcp in Claude Code and sign in. We have not tested Claude on the web, ChatGPT, Copilot Studio or the other assistants ourselves yet.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: What the other pages on this topic explain
paragraphs: Pages of their own explain setup in Claude Code, in Claude on the web and desktop, in Copilot Studio and in ChatGPT, VS Code or Cursor, running it on a self-hosted instance, choosing between a key and the browser sign-in, allowing and disconnecting assistants, and the messages an assistant gets when it may not do something. Security, data protection and prompt injection (instructions hidden in data) each have a page.

Two pages cover whether AI can implement NIS 2 for you and who answers for what it enters. What an assistant fills in is set out item by item on its own page, with pages on your list in 2.2, on suppliers, on risks, on policies and on evidence. Then there is the comparison with a chat, and a page on tracing its entries.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: You see the assistant most clearly on the lists the walkthrough starts with.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks what your inventory shows and records what each entry is exactly and who provides it. You check each list and finish.
5.1 Write down who works for you: it creates the suppliers from your accounts payable list. In the app you remove anything that is not a supplier.
Every screen an assistant wrote carries a mark such as “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”.
7.3 Record the management review: no assistant fills in anything here. A person records the management review in the app, and management approves.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 2.2, screen “Software for customers, staff and money”. At the top the mark “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”, below it the note that the entry “Warenwirtschaft (ERP)” is on your list.

items.q: Is MCP the same as an API?
items.a: Not quite. An API is an interface each program builds its own way. MCP sets out how an AI assistant finds and calls such tools, so it can use many programs in the same way. Behind the nisd2.eu MCP server are the same functions the app itself calls.

items.q: Is the MCP server itself an AI?
items.a: No. The server takes your assistant's calls, checks them and saves what the app would save. The AI is the assistant your company chose.

items.q: Does every person need their own connection?
items.a: Yes. An assistant always works as the person who connected it, with their rights. In Settings each person sees their connections and ends each one with “Disconnect”, or all at once with “Disconnect all assistants”.

items.q: Does it work with a self-hosted instance?
items.a: Yes, every instance has the server, and signing in needs no third-party service. Claude on the web, ChatGPT and Copilot Studio connect from their vendor's cloud, though, so your instance has to be reachable from the internet over https. Claude Code runs on your computer and also reaches an instance inside the company network.

meta.title: NIS 2 with AI: what an assistant can and cannot do
meta.description: An AI assistant can collect, sort and write down for NIS 2. Your company implements the measures and management approves them. What the law says about AI.

canAiImplement.title: Can AI implement NIS 2 for us?
canAiImplement.subtitle: Part of the work, yes. An assistant can collect facts, sort them, write them down and propose text. Your company carries out the measures, and management has to approve them (Art. 20(1) NIS 2).

sections.heading: What an assistant can take on
paragraphs: An AI assistant can gather facts that already exist and put them into the shape the walkthrough asks for. From an accounts payable list, an inventory or a licence overview it makes rows in a list. For a policy it picks the sections that apply and writes what else holds in your company.
That is what the NIS 2 walkthrough is built for: it asks item by item what needs recording, and a connected assistant enters it there.

sections.heading: What has to happen in the company
paragraphs: A measure is in place when it works in daily operations: when, say, the second factor is switched on at the sign-ins and the backup can really be restored. An assistant that fills in records can write this down. It cannot make it happen.

The decision stays with people too. Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the measures and oversees their implementation. In Germany, § 38(1) BSIG obliges management to implement the measures and oversee their implementation.

sections.heading: What NIS 2 says about AI
paragraphs: Little. The Directive names artificial intelligence in two recitals only, the reasoning that comes before the articles. Under recital 51, Member States should encourage AI where it could improve the detection and prevention of cyberattacks, in line with data protection law. Under recital 89, entities should evaluate their own cybersecurity capabilities and, where appropriate, bring in technology that improves security, such as AI or machine learning.

Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which sets out the measures in more detail for certain digital services, does not mention AI at all. Neither text says whether a risk analysis may be produced with the help of AI. The Directive requires management to approve the measures and oversee their implementation.
No authority has said whether it accepts NIS 2 records written with AI, as far as we could check (as of October 2026). We found no statement on it from the BSI, ENISA or national authorities.

sections.heading: Where an assistant helps in the walkthrough, and where it does not
paragraphs: It helps most with lists that already exist in another form. In 2.2 your inventory becomes the list of your software and technology, in 5.1 your accounts payable list becomes the list of your suppliers. In 2.1 it can adopt the risk assessment method the walkthrough proposes.

It helps little with facts that are written down nowhere. If no document records when a backup was last restored successfully, the assistant cannot know it. So the server instructs it to enter only what your records and systems show, and to leave a field empty rather than guess.
For two decisions it has no tool at all: whether your company decides not to do an item, and whether management approves the documents. People make those in the app.

sections.heading: When the assistant gets it wrong
paragraphs: A language model can invent facts or put them in the wrong place. In the walkthrough that could be a supplier that does not exist, or a backup schedule that is wrong. The server checks the form of an entry, for example that a date is a date. Whether it is true, it cannot know.
That is why a person finishes every item. Each screen an assistant wrote carries its name and the day. Read those screens before you finish, and correct in the app what is wrong.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: These items show where an assistant helps and where you decide.
points: 2.1 Decide how you rate risks: the assistant can adopt the proposed method. Read the explanation and the example matrix first, because the ratings in 2.3 rest on this method.
2.2 Write down what your company has: from your inventory it enters software, technology and providers. You check each list, remove in the app what is wrong, and finish.

The screen of every document, such as the security policy in 2.4, has the tick box “I have read the document, and it fits our company”. Only a person in the app can tick it, and the screen only lets them continue once it is ticked.
7.3 Record the management review: management approves the documents and signs off the items. No assistant has a tool for that.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 12.2, first step “Understand”: the explanation “Registering with your authority” in plain words, on the right the box “Often missed” and below it the provisions the item rests on, Art. 3 NIS 2 and § 33 Abs. 1 BSIG.
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, check it yourself

items.q: Does the BSI accept records written by AI?
items.a: The BSI has not said, and neither has ENISA or any other authority, as far as we could check (October 2026). The law asks whether the measures are in place and whether management approved them. It does not say who has to write a text.

items.q: Can the assistant fill in the whole walkthrough on its own?
items.a: No. It fills in fields, lists and texts, but a person finishes every item, and management approves at the end. In 7.3 it fills in nothing at all. What it enters should be checked by someone who knows your company.

items.q: What if the assistant makes something up?
items.a: Then it stands wrong in your records until someone corrects it. The mark on the screen shows which entries came from an assistant. Correct them in the app before you finish the item.

items.q: Does the AI Act apply to us if we use an assistant?
items.a: A company that uses an AI assistant at work is its deployer under Art. 3(4) AI Act. Art. 4 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 applies to deployers: measures that support the AI literacy of staff, with no specific level required. That filling in records is not a high-risk use is our reading, not an authority's.

items.q: Does an assistant help with registering with the BSI?
items.a: In 12.2 it can record what the registration produced: the user account ID of your organisation certificate and the date of registration. The registration itself happens in the BSI's portal, outside the walkthrough.

meta.title: NIS 2 and AI: who is accountable for the entries?
meta.description: An AI assistant enters data as the person who connected it. Management approves under Art. 20 NIS 2. What the AI Act asks of your company as a deployer.

accountability.title: Who answers for what the AI enters?
accountability.subtitle: An assistant enters data as the person who connected it, and every entry stands under that person's name. Management approves the measures and oversees their implementation (Art. 20(1) NIS 2). That is why no assistant can finish or approve an item in the walkthrough.

sections.heading: What the law gives to management
sections.law: Art. 20(1) NIS 2 · § 38(1) BSIG · Annex point 2.1.1 CIR (EU) 2024/2690
paragraphs: Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the risk management measures under Art. 21, oversees their implementation and can be held liable for infringements. In Germany, § 38(1) BSIG transposes this: management is obliged to implement the measures and oversee their implementation.

For certain digital services, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 goes further. Under point 2.1.1 of its Annex, management accepts the risk assessment results and the residual risks, or an accountable person who reports to it.
None of these provisions mentions AI. The duty to approve and oversee stays with management, whoever filled in a field.

sections.heading: Whose entry is it?
paragraphs: In the walkthrough an assistant works as the person who connected it, with exactly their rights. What it saves appears in the activity log under that person's name, with “via” and the assistant's name.

In the walkthrough, then, it is that person's entry. They connected the assistant and can disconnect it in Settings at any time. With the switch “Allow AI assistants for this company” an admin can turn assistants off for the whole company, which ends every connection.

sections.heading: Why the assistant cannot approve
paragraphs: Approval belongs to management, so the MCP server has no tool for it. An assistant cannot finish an item, cannot record that the company decided not to do one, and cannot approve anything. That holds for a managing director's assistant too.

At 7.3 only someone who has been assigned the team role “CEO / Managing Director” can approve, signed in with their own account. The name and the date of the approval then stand on each document they approved.

sections.heading: What the AI Act says
sections.law: Art. 3(4), Art. 4 and Annex III AI Act
paragraphs: A company that uses an AI assistant at work is the “deployer” of that system under Art. 3(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act. The duties for high-risk systems attach, among other things, to the uses Annex III lists.

Our reading, not an authority's: an assistant that fills in records for your NIS 2 obligations is not a safety component of critical infrastructure under Annex III point 2, and the other points there do not describe this use either. On the text, the high-risk duties therefore do not apply.

Every deployer is covered by Art. 4 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. It asks for measures that support the AI literacy of the staff who work with the system, and no specific level. An obvious start: whoever connects the assistant knows that it can be wrong, and how to check its entries.

sections.heading: Management has to understand what it approves
paragraphs: Approving and overseeing assume that management understands what it decides on. Art. 20(2) NIS 2 fits here: members of management have to follow training. In Germany, § 38(3) BSIG requires management to take part in training regularly.

In the walkthrough this is item 1.1, management training. An assistant can record there who was trained when, and upload the certificate if it can send files itself. Management has to take part itself.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: In the walkthrough, accountability shows in two places: training at the start and approval at the end.
points: 1.1 Get management trained: an assistant records who in management was trained when. Management attends the training itself.
Before finishing each item, a person reads the screens that carry an assistant's mark and corrects in the app what is wrong.
7.3 Record the management review: management sees its risks and the open points, each with a record of who takes care of it and by when, and approves the documents. Name and date are recorded.
After that, the server refuses an assistant's change to a list a signed item rests on. A person makes such changes in the app, and the item goes back to management.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 7.3, screen “Management approves the documents”: the documents the walkthrough wrote, each marked “Approved on 3 October 2026 by Claudia Lohse”.
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, prepare approval

items.q: Can management leave the approval to its assistant?
items.a: Not in the walkthrough. There is no tool for it, not for a managing director's assistant either. Management approves in the app, with its own account, and its name and the date then stand on each approved document.

items.q: Who answers if the assistant enters something wrong?
items.a: In the walkthrough the entry stands under the name of the person who connected the assistant. Your NIS 2 obligations do not change: management approves the measures and oversees their implementation. That is why a person should check every item before finishing it.

items.q: Do we have to train staff in using AI?
items.a: Since the amendment by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 4 AI Act asks for measures that support your staff's AI literacy. You do not have to guarantee a specific level. A short briefing on what the assistant may do, where it can be wrong and how to check its entries is an obvious start.

items.q: Is our assistant a high-risk system?
items.a: In our reading, not while it fills in records: it is not a safety component under Annex III point 2 AI Act. No authority has commented on this use so far, as far as we can see. If you use the same assistant for other things too, check those uses separately.

meta.title: AI assistant in the NIS 2 walkthrough: what it fills
meta.description: Screen by screen: what a connected AI assistant may fill in the NIS 2 walkthrough, what stays in the app, and which rules hold for every item.

whatItFills.title: What an assistant fills in the walkthrough, and what it does not
whatItFills.subtitle: An assistant fills in fields, lists, ratings, agreements, sign-ins, backups and the text of the policies, in items that are open or on the waiting list. Finishing, every decision, deleting suppliers, assets or trainings, and everything at 7.3 stay in the app.

sections.heading: The rules for every item
paragraphs: An assistant writes only into items that are open or on the waiting list. If it works on an item on the waiting list, it picks it up again, as the app does. An item that is finished, decided against or signed is changed by a person in the app.

The server refuses an empty answer, so that no assistant erases what someone wrote. A field it leaves out stays as it is. It never deletes a supplier, an asset or a training. The crypto list in 9.1 works differently, more on that below. If a signed item rests on a list, the server refuses any change to that list and names the items affected.
If a person holds the Reviewer or Legal reviewer access role in the team, their assistant only reads. Everyone else fills in items in the categories assigned to them, an admin in all of them.

sections.heading: Fields and lists
paragraphs: Fields are the single questions of an item. An assistant answers them in 12.2 (account reference, date of registration), 3.1 (who leads in an emergency, the emergency number, how you reach each other when email and the network are down, whom the person leading calls next), 3.3 (whether you can sign in to the portal and report), 11.2 (tools for phone, video and chat), 6.3 (address for vulnerability reports) and 12.4 (attack detection system, last evidence sent to the BSI).

It fills lists in 1.1 and 8.2, who was trained when, and in 5.1, your suppliers. It adds rows and corrects existing ones. For a supplier linked through its own account, it cannot change the statements the supplier made itself.

sections.heading: What your company has, and how risky it is
paragraphs: In 2.2 it ticks on four screens what your company has: “What your company does every day”, “Software for customers, staff and money”, “Software everyone uses” and “Technology and rooms”. It adds entries of your own as well. On the two screens after that it records which software or device it is exactly, where it runs and who provides it. A provider not yet on your supplier list is added there.

In 2.1 it can adopt the risk assessment method the walkthrough proposes. In 2.3 it rates software, technology and suppliers: how often something could happen and how badly it would hit, with a short note if wanted. The risk map only shows the result.

sections.heading: Contracts, sign-ins, backups and processes
paragraphs: In 5.2 it records for each supplier whether the contract settles security and whether it provides for incident notification. In 11.1 it records for each sign-in whether it takes a second factor, and which one.

In 4.4 it notes for each backup system how often it backs up and on which day a restore last worked. In 4.2 it marks which processes must keep running without IT, with a line on how. Each row is saved as it sends it, which is why the server tells it to read what is there first.

sections.heading: Policies and the crypto list
paragraphs: Six items write a document: 3.1, 2.4, 9.1, 10.1, 6.3 and 4.2. An assistant picks which sections of the template apply to your company and writes what else holds there. What is saved is a draft, which management approves at 7.3.
Once management has approved a document, no assistant rewrites it, because a changed text loses the approval. That happens in the app.

In 9.1 it takes over the list of accepted methods the walkthrough proposes, and can adapt it to your company. When it changes the list, it sends the whole list as it should stand afterwards: a method it leaves out is no longer on the list. So read the list in the app before you finish 9.1.

sections.heading: What stays in the app
paragraphs: The assistant has no tool for these steps: finishing an item, putting it on the waiting list, recording that the company decided not to do it, deleting a supplier, an asset or a training, inviting someone. At 7.3 it fills in nothing. The management review, who takes care of open points by when, and the approval stay with people.

Only an assistant that can send a file itself, such as Claude Code, uploads a file as evidence. With other assistants you upload in the app. In 12.3 there is nothing to fill in: you read the item and finish it yourself.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Four items show how far an assistant goes and where you take over.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks entries on the four lists and describes each one. You read each list, remove in the app what is wrong, and finish.
5.2 Record what you have agreed with your suppliers: it records for each supplier what the contract settles. What follows from that, you decide.
4.4 Record your backups: it records how often backups run and when a restore last worked. A date nobody knows is better left empty until someone has tried a restore.
11.1 Record where a second factor protects: it records for each sign-in whether a second factor applies. A sign-in without one ends up on the list management sees at 7.3 before approving.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 2.2, screen “Software for customers, staff and money”. At the top the mark “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”, below it the note that the entry “Warenwirtschaft (ERP)” is on your list.
walk.next: Create an account and start

items.q: Can the assistant finish an item once everything is filled in?
items.a: No, there is no tool for that. The server tells it what was saved and which fields are still empty, with the link to the item in the app. A person finishes it there.

items.q: What happens if I ask it to change a signed item?
items.a: The server refuses and tells the assistant that the change is made in the app, with the link to it. That way no assistant takes back a management signature.

items.q: Why does it not enter a management review at 7.3?
items.a: A review recorded there puts the item before management. That would finish it without the person working on it having decided so. That is why a person records the management review in the app.

items.q: Can it fill in items assigned to a colleague?
items.a: Only if you may work on that category yourself, because you are an admin or it is assigned to you. An assistant never has more rights than the person who connected it.

meta.title: MCP or chat: filling in NIS 2 records with AI
meta.description: Chat or connected AI assistant: who writes where, what gets checked and logged, and which data reaches the vendor. With what Anthropic states about it.

mcpVsChat.title: MCP or a chat with uploaded documents?
mcpVsChat.subtitle: A chat gives you text that you paste somewhere yourself. An assistant connected over MCP writes straight into the walkthrough's lists, through the same checks as the app, under your name and marked on the screen. For a draft you read and paste in yourself, a chat is fine.

sections.heading: What happens in a chat
paragraphs: You upload an accounts payable list or an inventory to a chat and ask for a supplier list. Back comes text or a table. You copy it into your records by hand, row by row.

The chat knows only what you uploaded, as it stood on the day you uploaded it. What a colleague added to the walkthrough yesterday, it does not see. And later nobody can tell which row came from the chat and which one a person wrote.

sections.heading: What a connected assistant does differently
paragraphs: An assistant connected over MCP can read the current state of your walkthrough before it writes: the answers so far and the rows already on a list. Then it enters each fact where it belongs.

Every entry goes through the same checks as in the app; a date has to be a date, for example. Two more rules apply to assistants: the server refuses an empty answer, and it does not change a signed item. What does not fit goes back to the assistant with the reason.
It saves as you, with your rights. The activity log shows the change under your name with “via” and the assistant's name, and the screen shows which assistant wrote it on which day.

sections.heading: Where your data goes
paragraphs: If the model runs at a vendor, that vendor sees what the assistant works with in both cases. In a chat that is what you upload or paste, over MCP it is what the assistant reads from the walkthrough. Both run under your company's agreement with that vendor. If the assistant and the model run on your own hardware, nothing leaves your network.

Anthropic describes one difference for Claude. Feedback data, meaning what you send with the thumbs up or down button, does not include raw content from connectors, including remote and local MCP servers, “though data may be included if it's directly copied into your conversation with Claude”. For its commercial products Anthropic also states that inputs and outputs are not used for training by default.
We have not checked the terms of OpenAI or Microsoft. Read your company's agreement with them.

sections.heading: When a chat is fine
paragraphs: For a text you read and paste in yourself anyway, a chat does the job. The security policy in 2.4, for example, has the field “Anything else that applies at your company (optional)”. You can have a chat draft that, read it, and copy it into the field.
Give the chat only what it needs for the wording, then. It does not need names, network diagrams or credentials for that.
For lists with many rows, and for facts someone should be able to trace later, a connected assistant has more going for it.

sections.heading: What MCP does not solve
paragraphs: A connected assistant can be wrong just as a chat can. The mark on the screen shows you where to look, and you finish the item yourself.

Text in your records can also contain sentences a model takes for instructions. This is called prompt injection. In its baseline protection against indirect prompt injections (version 1.0, 14.09.2026) the BSI recalls that no reliable countermeasure exists that removes the problem completely.
The server tells the assistant to treat everything it reads as data, and it marks filling in as a step that changes data. Choose an assistant that asks you before such a step.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: The difference shows in the lists at the start of the walkthrough and in the security policy.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks the entries directly and describes them. You type nothing, but you do check.
Each of these changes then appears in the activity log under your name, with “via” and the assistant's name.
2.4 Write the security policy: both work here. An assistant picks the sections and writes what else applies, or you copy a draft from a chat into the field.
Either way the policy stays a draft until management approves it at 7.3.
walk.seeItAlt: The activity log, day by day: entries such as “Walkthrough item finished”, “Documents approved” and “Signed off by management”, each with the person's name and the time on the right.

items.q: Does the vendor see less of our data with MCP?
items.a: Not as such. What the assistant reads goes to its vendor, so the model can work with it. The difference lies in what you copy into a conversation yourself, and with Anthropic in what can end up in feedback data.

items.q: May a connected assistant do more than a chat?
items.a: Yes, it may write in your walkthrough, as you. That is why an admin first turns on “Allow AI assistants for this company”, and each person can disconnect theirs in Settings. A chat without a connection changes nothing in your records.

items.q: Can I use MCP in Claude on the web or in ChatGPT too?
items.a: Yes, if you add the MCP server there as a custom connector. Both connect from their vendor's cloud and use the browser sign-in; according to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot present a custom key. In Claude, choose the option Anthropic labels “Register automatically”, since of Claude's options it is the only one our sign-in server supports. So far we have tested Claude Code, not these two.

items.q: Which is better for a first supplier list?
items.a: If your accounts payable list exists as a file, a connected assistant. It creates the suppliers in 5.1 directly in the list that 2.3 and 5.2 need later. You check the list and remove in the app anything that is not a supplier.

meta.title: Allow AI assistants: the switch in Settings
meta.description: Whether your people may connect an AI assistant to the NIS 2 walkthrough is an admin's decision. Where the switch is, and what turning it off ends.

allowAssistants.title: Allowing assistants in your company
allowAssistants.subtitle: Whether people in your company may connect an AI assistant to the NIS 2 walkthrough is decided by an admin in Settings. Until an admin turns it on, it is off. When an admin turns it off again, every existing connection ends.

sections.heading: Where is the switch?
paragraphs: Open the profile menu with your name at the bottom left and choose "Settings". At the top is the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company".

It applies to the company that is open. When it is on, everyone in that company may connect their own assistant, for example Claude Code, Claude or Copilot Studio. The assistant then reads the walkthrough with the company's data and fills in what its items ask for.

It works as the person who connected it, with that person's rights: in their areas, or in all of them for an admin. The assistant of someone who only reviews the walkthrough can read it but fills in nothing.

sections.heading: Who may turn it on?
paragraphs: Only an admin of the company. Everyone else sees the switch locked, with the line "Only admins can change settings." below it.
An assistant cannot turn it on. The list of functions an assistant may call contains neither the switch nor creating a key.

Often the admin connects the first assistant themselves. If an assistant asks for access while the switch is off, the page for allowing it shows an admin the switch right there. Someone who is not an admin reads on that page that the admin has not allowed AI assistants, and can only decline.

sections.heading: What turning it off ends
paragraphs: The app checks the switch when someone creates a key or allows an assistant in the browser. After that it checks it again on every single call an assistant makes.

When an admin turns it off, every member's connections end: each key and each sign-in through the browser. The next call from an assistant is refused. For someone who belongs to several companies, this also ends their assistants in the other companies, and they connect them there again.
Turning it on again later does not bring those connections back, and each person connects their assistant again. What assistants have already entered stays in the walkthrough, with its mark.

sections.heading: Who can use an assistant at all
paragraphs: An assistant works in the NIS 2 walkthrough, so only someone who may open the walkthrough can connect one: on nisd2.eu an account whose order includes the walkthrough, on a self-hosted instance the accounts with the addresses in PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS.

Anyone who may not open the walkthrough sees neither a key nor "Allow" in Settings or on the page for allowing an assistant, and gets the way to the walkthrough instead. An assistant that tries anyway is refused on every call.

sections.heading: Why the switch starts off
paragraphs: What an assistant reads goes to that assistant's vendor, under your company's agreement with them. Which vendor receives the data from your walkthrough is the company's decision. That is why an admin turns the switch on, and until then it stays off.
The switch covers every assistant. Which one a person connects is their own choice. So decide beforehand which assistants your company allows, and list them as software in 2.2, as described below.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Once you allow assistants, the assistant itself belongs in your walkthrough.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": add the assistant on "Software everyone uses", and its vendor on "Which software exactly, and from whom?".
5.1 "Write down who works for you": a vendor you name in 2.2 is already on this list. Add what they do for you, for example that they process the walkthrough data the assistant reads.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day, for example "Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026". The person checks it before finishing the item.
Finishing, deciding and signing stay in the app, even with the switch on.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu: at the top the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Go to the walkthrough, allow assistants

items.q: Can I allow assistants for some people only?
items.a: No, the switch applies to the whole company. What an assistant may do depends on the person who connects it, though: on their areas and their role. Each person sees their own connections in Settings under "Connected" and disconnects them there.

items.q: Does anyone notice when an assistant is connected in their name?
items.a: Yes. When a key is created or an assistant allowed in the browser, the person gets an email. For a sign-in through the browser it names the assistant and the address it returns to. It also says what to do if it was not them: disconnect all assistants and change the password.

items.q: Is the switch on a self-hosted instance too?
items.a: Yes. Every instance has the same switch and the same address for assistants, /api/mcp, and there is nothing to set up for it. There, the accounts whose addresses are in PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS can connect.

items.q: Is it recorded who flipped the switch?
items.a: Yes. Every change is in the activity log, under the admin's name. When it is turned off, the entry notes that every connection was ended.

items.q: May an assistant finish or sign anything once the switch is on?
items.a: No. The switch allows reading and filling in. Finishing an item, deciding it is not applicable or deliberately not done, and management's signature exist only in the app. No tool of an assistant can do them.

meta.title: Connect Claude Code to the NIS 2 walkthrough (MCP)
meta.description: One command in the terminal, one sign-in in the browser: how Claude Code reads and fills your NIS 2 walkthrough over MCP. Plus the key for scripts.

claudeCode.title: Connecting Claude Code to the NIS 2 walkthrough
claudeCode.subtitle: One command adds the walkthrough to Claude Code as an MCP server. Then you sign in through the browser and allow access. From then on Claude Code reads your items and fills in what they ask for; finishing and signing stay in the app.

sections.heading: What you need first
paragraphs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a protocol an AI assistant uses to talk to other software. Every instance offers an address for it; on nisd2.eu it is https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp.
An admin has turned on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in Settings, and your account has access to the walkthrough. Claude Code is installed on your computer.
Claude Code runs on your computer and connects from there, so it also reaches a self-hosted instance inside the company network. Put that instance's address in the commands instead of nisd2.eu.

sections.heading: Connecting with a sign-in through the browser
paragraphs: The command below adds the server to Claude Code. Then start Claude Code, type /mcp and follow the steps in your browser.

After you sign in, the nisd2.eu page shows which assistant asks for which company and where the browser returns to. For Claude Code that is localhost with a port number, your own computer: Claude Code receives the answer there itself.

Click "Allow". If your last sign-in was more than 15 minutes ago, the page first asks you to sign in again and then brings you back. The reason: an assistant stays connected even after you sign out of the browser.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: Connecting with a key
paragraphs: For scripts, or a computer without a browser, click "Create key" in Settings. The key is shown only at that moment. It lasts 90 days, in the company that was open when you made it.

Put it in the environment variable NISD2_MCP_KEY and add the server with the command below. The shell fills in the value when you run it, so for this command your history holds only the variable's name.

Unless you say otherwise, Claude Code stores the server and its key in the file ~/.claude.json in your home folder. Do not use the project scope for this: it writes to the file .mcp.json in the project, which Anthropic intends to be checked into the repository. A key belongs in no file you share.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $NISD2_MCP_KEY"

sections.heading: A first task
paragraphs: Give Claude Code a file from your own records and an item. For 5.1 the list of creditors from your accounting fits, since almost everyone who works for you sends you invoices. An example request is below.

To fill an item in, Claude Code needs the item with its fields and the rows already on the list; the tool get_walkthrough returns both. In "Manual" mode, according to Anthropic, Claude Code asks for permission the first time it uses each tool. Under /permissions the rule mcp__nisd2__get_walkthrough allows reading for good. Let filling in keep asking, so you confirm each change yourself.

We ran Claude Code end to end in our own test on a local instance, with the browser sign-in and with a key. In the test on 14.10.2026 it read the walkthrough, filled in four items, left the rest open and signed nothing.
sections.code: Read item 5.1 of the NIS 2 walkthrough and add the suppliers from creditors.csv. Leave empty whatever the file does not show.

sections.heading: What stays with you afterwards
paragraphs: Every screen Claude Code wrote carries a mark such as "Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026". The activity log shows each change under your name, "via" the assistant's name.

Finishing, deciding an item is not applicable and signing exist only in the app. Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2 the management body, in a GmbH its managing directors, approves the measures and oversees their implementation; in Germany, § 38(1) BSIG obliges management to implement them and oversee their implementation. The walkthrough is built on that: no tool of an assistant can finish or sign an item.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Good first items are those whose answers already sit in your files.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": from an inventory list or a licence overview, Claude Code ticks software and devices and enters on "Which software exactly, and from whom?" who provides them.
5.1 "Write down who works for you": the providers from 2.2 are already there. From the list of creditors, Claude Code adds the others, one line each with what they do for you.
4.4 "Record your backups": for each backup system on your list, Claude Code enters how often it backs up and when a restore from it last worked. If none has worked yet, the field stays empty.
Then you open each item in the app, check the marked screens and finish it.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect Claude Code

items.q: Can Claude Code upload files too?
items.a: It is built for that, since Claude Code can send a file's bytes itself. The tool upload_file gives an address to upload to, then Claude Code attaches the file to the item, as evidence or as the certificate of a training. A file counts as evidence only once it is stored at its full size. We have not yet tested uploading with Claude Code itself.

items.q: Do I have to explain to Claude Code what NIS 2 requires?
items.a: No. For each item, get_walkthrough returns the walkthrough's own words, its fields with their schema and what is already entered. The server also gives every assistant instructions, such as entering only what your records show and leaving a field out when in doubt.

items.q: I belong to several companies. Which one does Claude Code work for?
items.a: The company that was open in the app when you allowed it or created the key. For another company, switch company in the app and connect again.

items.q: Does Claude Code stay connected when I sign out?
items.a: Yes. You disconnect in Settings under "Connected": one at a time with "Disconnect", or all at once with "Disconnect all assistants". Changing your password also disconnects every assistant.

items.q: How many calls are allowed?
items.a: 300 tool calls per person per hour, for all of that person's assistants together. Beyond that the server answers that there were too many calls in the last hour. The next hourly window starts fresh.

meta.title: Connect Claude to the NIS 2 walkthrough: custom connector
meta.description: Add the NIS 2 walkthrough to Claude on the web and desktop as a custom connector, and why the instance must be reachable from the internet for it.

claude.title: Connecting Claude on the web and desktop
claude.subtitle: In Claude, add a custom connector with the address https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp, choose "Register automatically" and allow access. Claude connects from Anthropic's cloud, so the instance has to be reachable from the internet. We have not tested this route ourselves yet; the steps follow Anthropic's help pages as of 16.10.2026.

sections.heading: Before you start
paragraphs: In Claude, a connector is the link to an MCP server. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the protocol an AI assistant uses to talk to other software, and every instance of the walkthrough offers an address for it.
An admin has turned on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in Settings, and your account has access to the walkthrough.

According to Anthropic, custom connectors are available on the Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans; Free allows one. On Team and Enterprise an Owner adds the connector for the organisation, then each person connects themselves.

sections.heading: Adding the connector
paragraphs: On Pro and Max, open "Customize", then "Connectors", then "+ Add" and "Add custom connector". Enter a name, for example nisd2, and the address below.

Under "Authentication", choose "Sign in now" or "Sign in when needed". Under "OAuth client", which asks how Claude identifies itself as a client, choose "Register automatically". The recommended option "Use Claude's published identity" relies on a method the walkthrough's sign-in service does not offer.

On Team and Enterprise the Owner goes to "Organization settings", "Connectors", "Add", "Custom" and "Web" and enters the same details. Everyone else then finds the connector under "Customize", "Connectors" and clicks "Connect". All labels in quotes are those in Anthropic's English help; a German interface may name them differently.

sections.heading: Signing in and allowing
paragraphs: Claude opens the nisd2.eu sign-in page. After you sign in, it shows which assistant asks for which company and where the browser returns to. The assistant gives its name itself, so check the return address: it should belong to Anthropic.
Click "Allow". If your last sign-in was more than 15 minutes ago, you sign in again first and come back to the same page.

Claude never sees your password in this. It gets a token, a kind of pass with an expiry date. The token lasts an hour, and with a second token Claude can renew it itself until 90 days after your "Allow". Then you allow Claude again.

sections.heading: Why Claude has to reach the instance from the internet
paragraphs: According to Anthropic, Claude connects to the server from Anthropic's cloud, not from your computer. That holds on the web and in the desktop app alike.

nisd2.eu is reachable from the internet over https. A self-hosted instance that runs only inside the company network cannot be reached by Claude this way. For Enterprise, Anthropic describes tunnels into private networks, as a preview on request. Otherwise use Claude Code inside the company network, which runs on the computer.

sections.heading: What Claude fills in, and what stays in the app
paragraphs: Claude reads the items and fills in what they ask for, with your rights. It works best when you give it a list you already have in the chat and name the item.

A file as evidence needs an assistant that sends the file's bytes to storage itself. We have not tested whether Claude can do that from the chat, so upload evidence in the app. Finishing and signing stay there too.

According to Anthropic, under "Customize", "Connectors" you can set a single tool of the connector to "Blocked", for example fill_walkthrough_item, the tool that fills in, while Claude should only read.

Anthropic states that it does not use inputs and outputs of its commercial products, such as Claude for Work, for training by default, and that it acts as a processor there. Personal accounts come with their own terms; check those yourself.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: In a chat, work item by item, with a list you already have.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": with an inventory list in the chat, Claude ticks on the four lists what applies to you and enters who provides it.

3.1 "Plan what happens in an incident": on "Your emergency contacts", Claude enters who leads in an emergency, the IT emergency number, how you reach each other without email and network, and whom the person leading calls next.
From these answers the walkthrough writes your incident response plan. Claude can add below it what fits your company; read the plan in the app before you finish the item.
Every screen Claude wrote shows the assistant's name and the day.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect Claude

items.q: Can I enter a key in Claude instead of signing in?
items.a: Anthropic describes "Request headers" for API keys as a beta for a limited set of organisations. It recommends them for credentials a whole organisation shares, and the sign-in where each person uses their own account. The key from Settings belongs to one person, so use the browser sign-in for Claude.

items.q: Why does "Use Claude's published identity" not work?
items.a: With that option Claude identifies itself through a document Anthropic publishes on the internet (a Client ID Metadata Document). The walkthrough's sign-in service supports only automatic registration under RFC 7591. The MCP specification recommends the newer method and keeps automatic registration for servers that do not offer it.

items.q: We self-host inside the company network. How do we use Claude?
items.a: With a custom connector only if the instance is reachable from the internet over https, or through a tunnel that Anthropic describes for Enterprise as a preview on request. Claude Code connects from the computer and reaches the instance inside the company network directly.

items.q: What does Anthropic get to see of our data?
items.a: What Claude reads from the walkthrough goes to Anthropic, under your company's agreement with Anthropic. That is the items Claude reads for your request. The data protection article in this section of the wiki covers it in more detail.

items.q: Can Claude finish or sign an item?
items.a: No. No tool of an assistant finishes an item, decides one or signs. That stays in the app, and there only management can sign.

meta.title: Connect Copilot Studio to the NIS 2 walkthrough (MCP)
meta.description: Add the NIS 2 walkthrough as an MCP server in Microsoft Copilot Studio: Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.0 with Dynamic discovery and an instance on https.

copilotStudio.title: Connecting Microsoft Copilot Studio
copilotStudio.subtitle: In Copilot Studio you add the walkthrough as a tool of an agent, with the address https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp and OAuth 2.0 with "Dynamic discovery" for sign-in. Copilot Studio runs in Microsoft's cloud, so as we understand it the instance has to be reachable from the internet over https. We have not tested this route yet.

sections.heading: Who this suits
paragraphs: Copilot Studio is Microsoft's tool for an IT team to build its own agents. If your IT already works with Microsoft 365, it is an obvious place to bring the walkthrough in.

An agent here is an assistant your IT sets up in Copilot Studio. Through MCP (Model Context Protocol), the protocol for such connections, the walkthrough becomes one of its tools. The agent then reads your items and fills in what they ask for, as the person who signed in.

Before that, an admin has turned on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in the nisd2.eu Settings. We have not tested Copilot Studio against the walkthrough yet. The steps follow Microsoft's guide as of 15.10.2026.

sections.heading: Adding the server
paragraphs: In the agent, open the Tools page, then "Add a tool", "New tool" and "Model Context Protocol". The MCP onboarding wizard opens.

Fill in Server name, Server description and Server URL, with the address below. The agent reads the description to decide when to call the server, so say what it is for, for example: Reads and fills in the company's NIS 2 walkthrough.
According to Microsoft, Copilot Studio currently supports the Streamable HTTP transport, and has not supported the older SSE transport since August 2025. The walkthrough answers over Streamable HTTP.

sections.heading: Signing in with OAuth 2.0 and Dynamic discovery
paragraphs: OAuth is the usual way for software to sign in on your behalf without knowing your password. Choose OAuth 2.0 as the authentication type and "Dynamic discovery" as its type. Copilot Studio then finds the sign-in addresses itself and registers with the sign-in service that every instance runs itself.

Select "Create", then "Next". On "Add tool", create a connection with "Create a new connection" and add the server with "Add to agent". Connecting opens the nisd2.eu sign-in page: sign in, check where the browser returns to, "Allow".

According to Microsoft, with OAuth 2.0 the individual users of the agent sign in themselves and grant it permission. In the walkthrough the agent then works with the rights of the person who signed in.

Copilot Studio also offers an API key, in a header or as a query in the address. The walkthrough expects the key in the Authorization header, as "Bearer", a space, then the key; it does not accept it in the address. We have not checked whether Copilot Studio sends the header in that form. So use OAuth 2.0.

sections.heading: Does the instance have to be reachable from the internet?
paragraphs: Copilot Studio is a service in Microsoft's cloud. So we assume that Microsoft opens the connection to the walkthrough and that the instance has to be reachable from the internet over https. Microsoft's guide does not say so explicitly. nisd2.eu is reachable that way.

A self-hosted instance that runs only inside the company network would then not be reachable along the route in this article. We have not checked whether Microsoft offers a way into the company network for it. Inside the company network, software that runs on the computer works, such as Claude Code.

In Copilot Studio, access to MCP servers runs through the Power Platform: according to Microsoft, a data policy for connectors also governs the MCP server and its tools. Ask whoever manages the Power Platform at your company whether a policy allows the server.

sections.heading: What the agent may do, and what not
paragraphs: The agent reads the items and fills in fields, lists and screens, with the signed-in person's rights. It cannot finish an item, decide it is not applicable, delete a row or sign, because the server offers those functions to no assistant.
What the agent reads goes to Microsoft, under your company's agreement with Microsoft. We did not check Microsoft's terms on this for this article.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: For an IT team that works in Microsoft 365, two items suggest themselves.
points: 5.1 "Write down who works for you": the agent adds to your list of suppliers, one line each with what they do for you. The item counts everyone who can reach your data, so Microsoft as the agent's vendor belongs there too.

10.1 "Write the staff, access and asset policy": the template has fixed sections on joining, changing role and leaving, on outside staff, on access and on managing your IT. The agent picks the clauses that fit and adds below what applies to you, for example how Microsoft 365 accounts are blocked on the last working day.
Every screen the agent wrote shows its name and the day. The person reads the policy in the app and finishes the item there; management approves it, in the app as well.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect Copilot Studio

items.q: What rights does the agent get?
items.a: Those of the person who signs in: their areas of the walkthrough, or all of them for an admin. The agent of someone who only reviews the walkthrough can read it but fills in nothing.

items.q: How long does the agent stay connected?
items.a: With the refresh token the walkthrough hands out, Copilot Studio can renew the sign-in itself. It ends at the latest 90 days after "Allow", and then the person signs in again. A new password ends it sooner.

items.q: How do I end the connection?
items.a: In the nisd2.eu Settings under "Connected" with "Disconnect", or all at once with "Disconnect all assistants". For the whole company, an admin turns "Allow AI assistants for this company" off. The connection ends at its next call.

items.q: Is there a limit on calls?
items.a: Yes, 300 tool calls per person per hour, for all of that person's assistants together. The next hourly window starts fresh.

items.q: Can I see in the walkthrough what the agent entered?
items.a: Yes. Every screen it wrote carries its name and the day. The activity log shows each change under the person's name, "via" the agent's name.

meta.title: Connect ChatGPT, VS Code and Cursor to NIS 2 (MCP)
meta.description: Which assistants can read and fill in the NIS 2 walkthrough over MCP, what a client needs for it, and how to judge an assistant before you connect it.

otherAssistants.title: Connecting ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor and other assistants
otherAssistants.subtitle: An assistant that talks to an MCP server over Streamable HTTP and either signs in through the browser with automatic registration or sends a key in a header can read and fill in the walkthrough. We have not tested any of the assistants on this page ourselves; the steps follow the vendors' guides as of 16.10.2026.

sections.heading: What an assistant needs
paragraphs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the protocol an AI assistant uses to talk to other software. The assistant has to reach an MCP server over the network, using Streamable HTTP, at https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp or your own instance's address.

It can sign in two ways. Through the browser under OAuth 2.1 with automatic registration (Dynamic Client Registration): the person signs in and allows access. Or with a key from Settings, which it sends in the Authorization header as Bearer.
The walkthrough's sign-in service offers no other way, such as published client documents (Client ID Metadata Documents) or fixed client credentials. So far we have tested Claude Code.

sections.heading: ChatGPT
paragraphs: According to OpenAI, you go to Plugins in ChatGPT, select the plus button, then "Add custom MCP server". Your account and workspace policies apply; we could not check which plans it is enabled for.
According to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot present custom API keys. That leaves the browser sign-in, which ChatGPT supports with automatic registration.
For ChatGPT the server has to be reachable through a public https endpoint, or through the tunnel OpenAI offers for it (Secure MCP Tunnel). nisd2.eu is publicly reachable.

sections.heading: VS Code with GitHub Copilot
paragraphs: In VS Code you add the server to the file mcp.json, with the type http and the address. Microsoft advises against hardcoding API keys there and points to input variables or environment files instead.
VS Code runs on your computer, so it also reaches an instance inside the company network. For some servers it shows a dialog on first start, where you decide whether to trust it.

sections.heading: Cursor and Gemini CLI
paragraphs: Cursor speaks Streamable HTTP. For OAuth sign-in, its guide names fixed client credentials as the exception for servers without automatic registration. The walkthrough offers automatic registration, so the browser sign-in should work; we have not tested it. Alternatively Cursor sends headers from its mcp.json, so it can send the key too, reading the value from an environment variable. According to Cursor, it asks for approval by default before using an MCP server's tools.

Gemini CLI signs in through the browser as soon as the server asks for it, and /mcp auth nisd2 starts the sign-in yourself. With a key, add the server as below. The option -s user stores it in your user settings (~/.gemini/settings.json); without it, according to Google, it lands in .gemini/settings.json in the project, key included.
Do not set trust to true for this server. According to Google, that makes Gemini CLI skip every confirmation before a tool call, including before filling in.
sections.code: gemini mcp add -s user --transport http --header "Authorization: Bearer $NISD2_MCP_KEY" nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: How to judge an assistant
paragraphs: Does it ask before it changes data? The tool that fills in is marked as one that changes data. A client that asks before such calls asks here. The MCP specification recommends that a person can deny any tool call.

Does it run on your computer or in the vendor's cloud? Software on the computer, such as VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Claude Code, also reaches an instance inside the company network. According to their vendors, ChatGPT and Claude on the web need an instance reachable from the internet, or a tunnel; for Copilot Studio we assume the same.

Where does the data go? What the assistant reads goes to the vendor of its model, even when the program itself runs on your computer, under your company's agreement with that vendor. If both the program and the model run on your own hardware, the walkthrough data stays in your network. The data protection article in this section of the wiki goes into it.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Whichever assistant you use, item 2.2 is a good first task.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has" has four lists to tick: what your company does every day, software for customers, staff and money, software everyone uses, and technology and rooms.
Then the item asks which software and which technology exactly, and from whom. A provider the assistant names there then appears on your supplier list in 5.1.
Give the assistant an inventory list and ask it to leave open whatever the list does not show. The server gives every assistant the same instruction.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day. You finish the item in the app.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect an assistant

items.q: Why does my key not work in ChatGPT?
items.a: According to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot present custom API keys. Use the browser sign-in there.

items.q: Are there European assistants that can do this?
items.a: Mistral Le Chat and Langdock describe their own connections to MCP servers in their documentation. We have checked neither the details nor a connection to the walkthrough. Judge whether they fit with the questions above.

items.q: What if my client cannot find the sign-in?
items.a: Without a key the server answers 401 and points to its description at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/api/mcp. From there a client finds the sign-in service and the automatic registration. If your client cannot do that, use the key.

items.q: How do we connect our own script or agent?
items.a: Use the key: it lasts 90 days, in one company, and is sent in the Authorization header as Bearer. The tools get_walkthrough, fill_walkthrough_item and upload_file describe their own inputs as JSON Schema.

items.q: Can an assistant delete anything?
items.a: It cannot delete: no tool deletes a row, finishes an item or signs. It can replace, though: an answer with a new one, and a row with a corrected one. It cannot empty a field. A person removes a wrong row in the app.

meta.title: MCP key or browser sign-in: what lasts how long
meta.description: Two ways to connect an AI assistant to the NIS 2 walkthrough: a sign-in through the browser or a key. How long each lasts, and what ends it.

keyOrSignIn.title: A key or a sign-in in the browser?
keyOrSignIn.subtitle: Sign an assistant in through the browser wherever it can: you copy no secret, and access renews itself until 90 days after your "Allow". Use the key for scripts and for software without a browser. It lasts 90 days and is shown only once.

sections.heading: Which way to choose?
paragraphs: The browser sign-in, wherever the client supports it. Claude Code, Claude on the web and desktop, Copilot Studio and ChatGPT describe it in their guides; according to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot send a key. So far we have tested Claude Code, both ways.
The key for scripts, your own agents and software that cannot open a browser. Keep it in an environment variable or a password manager, in no file you share or put in a repository.

sections.heading: The sign-in through the browser
paragraphs: The assistant opens your instance's sign-in page. You sign in, see which assistant asks for which company and where the browser returns to, and click "Allow".

Technically this is OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and automatic registration. OAuth is the way for software to sign in on your behalf without seeing your password. PKCE makes sure only the client that started the sign-in can collect the access. The instance is its own sign-in service, so even when self-hosted no third party is involved.

The assistant gets two tokens, passes with an expiry date. It calls the walkthrough with the access token, which lasts an hour. With the refresh token it gets a new access token. The refresh token lasts 30 days, and every renewal replaces it with a new one.
At the latest 90 days after your "Allow", the sign-in ends, however often the assistant renewed. Then you allow it again.

sections.heading: When a refresh token turns up twice
paragraphs: If the same refresh token comes in again within a minute, the server still accepts it. That happens when a client renews twice at once, or an answer is lost on the way.

If it comes in again later, the server treats it as copied. It then disconnects every assistant of that person, the key included, and the person connects again. If the original and a copy both renewed within that minute, it shows once both renew again.

sections.heading: The key
paragraphs: In Settings, "Create key" makes a key. It is shown only at that moment and stored nowhere, so the app cannot show it again.
It lasts 90 days, as you and with your role, in the company that was open when you made it. The client sends it in the Authorization header as Bearer.
You hold one key per company. A new one ends the previous key; assistants that signed in through the browser stay connected.

sections.heading: Why both ask for a recent sign-in
paragraphs: Both survive signing out of the browser: an assistant stays connected even after you sign out. That is why "Create key" and "Allow" ask for a sign-in from the last 15 minutes. With an older session the page sends you to sign in and then brings you back.
The app tells you by email about every new connection. If it was not you, disconnect all assistants and change your password.

sections.heading: What ends a connection
paragraphs: "Disconnect" in Settings ends one connection at its next call; the others stay. "Disconnect all assistants" ends the key and every browser sign-in at once, and so does any change to your password: a new one, a first one, or removing it when you switch to signing in with Google.

If you leave the company or are removed, your key and sign-ins end for good; a later invitation does not bring them back. If an admin turns off "Allow AI assistants for this company", every member's connections end.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: How people sign in is itself an item of the walkthrough.
points: 11.1 "Record where a second factor protects": for each program and access on your list, the item records how people sign in: password only, with a second factor and which one, or not known yet.

A connected assistant can fill this in. Each row starts at "Password only", the safe assumption; give it a source, such as an overview from your account administration, and have it choose "Not known yet" where the source shows nothing.
List the assistant itself in 2.2 under "Software everyone uses", and 11.1 then also asks how you sign in to it.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day; you finish 11.1 in the app.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect an assistant

items.q: Can I connect several assistants at once?
items.a: Yes. Each browser sign-in is a connection of its own, plus one key per company. Settings lists them all under "Connected", with the day each was connected and last used, and each can be disconnected on its own.

items.q: What happens after 90 days?
items.a: The key stops working; create a new one and enter it in the client. A browser sign-in ends 90 days after "Allow", and then you allow the assistant again.

items.q: Does a key work for several companies?
items.a: No. It works in the company that was open when you made it. For another company, switch in the app and create a key there.

items.q: How is a key protected?
items.a: It is signed with a key the instance derives from AUTH_SECRET, and stored nowhere. Every call checks the signature, the expiry, whether the connection is still open and whether the person still belongs to the company. If a self-hosted instance rotates AUTH_SECRET, every key and sign-in ends.

meta.title: Asset inventory with an AI assistant: walkthrough item 2.2
meta.description: An AI assistant fills the lists in item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough from your inventory or licence list. What it enters, and what you check.

assets.title: Writing down what your company has, with an assistant
assets.subtitle: A connected AI assistant can fill the lists in item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough from your own records: tick entries in the catalogue, add your own and say who provides what. Every screen it wrote shows its name and the day. You check the list and finish the item in the app.

sections.heading: What item 2.2 asks of you
paragraphs: Item 2.2 is called “Write down what your company has”. It keeps four lists: “What your company does every day” (your processes), “Software for customers, staff and money”, “Software everyone uses” and “Technology and rooms”. Each list comes with a catalogue to tick, 132 entries in all, such as “Accounting software (DATEV, Lexware, sevDesk, lexoffice)” or “Laptops and desktops”. Anything missing you add as an entry of your own.

Two screens then ask for more detail: “Which software exactly, and from whom?” and “Which technology exactly, and from whom?”. For each entry they record what you actually use, what it does at your company, whether it runs in house or in the cloud, and who provides it. Every provider you name there goes onto your supplier list in item 5.1.

The directive counts policies on risk analysis and asset management among the minimum measures. In Germany, the BSIG asks for concepts for managing your ICT systems, products and processes. A list is the usual first step. A complete, up to date inventory is required in so many words by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, Annex point 12.4, which applies directly only to certain digital services, such as cloud and data centre providers.
sections.law: Art. 21(2)(a) and (i) NIS 2 · § 30(2) no. 1 and 9 BSIG

sections.heading: What the assistant does with your records
paragraphs: An AI assistant connects to your company in the app through MCP. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an assistant such as Claude read and enter data in an application. The assistant then works as the person who connected it, with that person's rights.

Give it what you already have: your IT provider's inventory, a licence list, or an export from your CMDB, the database where your IT keeps its devices and software. The assistant matches the lines to catalogue entries and ticks those. For the rest it adds entries of its own. On the two detail screens it records what exactly each thing is and who provides it. There, what it sends is what counts: if it leaves a provider out for a program, the two are no longer linked, and the provider stays on the supplier list.

The server tells every assistant to enter only what the company's own records and systems show, and to leave a field empty rather than guess. Whether it did, you can see on the list itself. That is why you check it.

sections.heading: What an assistant does not do here
paragraphs: It does not finish item 2.2, and it takes nothing off the list: none of its tools deletes an entry from this list. If something wrong is on it, you take it off in the app.
It works on items that are still open or that you set aside. Once you have finished 2.2, the server takes nothing more from the assistant on that item; you make changes to 2.2 in the app.

While an item that relies on this list is signed off, such as 2.2 itself or 4.4 on backups, the tools refuse any change the assistant makes to the list and name the items concerned. The change would take that sign-off back. That is a person's step in the app, and the item then goes to management again.

sections.heading: How you see what the assistant entered
paragraphs: Every screen an assistant wrote carries a mark at the top, for example “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”. The assistant gives that name itself. The mark stays when you change the screen afterwards, so it shows that an assistant entered data there even if you corrected it later.

The activity log lists every change under the name of the person who connected the assistant, with “via” and the assistant's name. That keeps changes made in the browser apart from changes made through the assistant.

Before you finish, go through all four lists and both detail screens. Look out for software you rent from the cloud, such as email or accounting. The walkthrough names it as often missed, and a plain device list will not contain it.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Item 2.2 turns into work on six screens, and item 2.3 builds directly on it.
points: 2.2, the four lists from “What your company does every day” to “Technology and rooms”: the assistant ticks catalogue entries and adds entries of its own from your records.

2.2, “Which software exactly, and from whom?” and “Which technology exactly, and from whom?”: it records what exactly each thing is, where it runs and who provides it. Those providers then appear on your supplier list in 5.1.
You go through every screen that carries the assistant's mark, take off what is wrong, add what is missing and finish 2.2 in the app.
2.3 “Rate your risks”: every piece of software and technology on the list gets a level from frequency and damage. Management signs off at the end, in 7.3.
walk.seeItAlt: Item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough, screen “Software for customers, staff and money”, with the assistant's mark at the top naming claude-code/2.1.287 and 16 October 2026, and the entry “Warenwirtschaft (ERP)” on the list
walk.next: Start your list in the walkthrough

items.q: Do I have to go through the whole catalogue myself?
items.a: No. You check what is on the list, add what is missing and take off what is wrong in the app. The walkthrough itself says the list does not have to be perfect: when something new comes along, you add it later.

items.q: Which records help the assistant most?
items.a: What your company already keeps: your IT provider's inventory, a licence list, a CMDB export. For the providers, the list of creditors helps, because the provider is whoever sends you the invoice. An assistant such as Claude Code runs on your computer and can read such files there. An assistant in the browser gets the file however it accepts files, for example as an attachment in the chat.

items.q: What happens to the providers the assistant names?
items.a: Every provider name not yet on your supplier list is added there as a new supplier. In item 5.1 it is already on the list. One call may name at most 50 different providers; for more, the assistant makes several calls.

items.q: Can the assistant delete an entry?
items.a: No. None of its three tools deletes an entry of the list in 2.2 or a row of a register. You take a wrong entry off the list in the app.

items.q: Does the vendor of my assistant see our list?
items.a: What the assistant reads goes to its vendor, under your company's agreement with that vendor. Which assistant you use is your choice. With an assistant and a model running on your own hardware, nothing leaves your network.
